name: Traditionalist conservatism
summary: Traditionalist conservatism holds that society rests on a transcendent moral order and on customs, institutions and hierarchies inherited across generations. It prizes family, religion, local community and property, prefers gradual change guided by prudence, and distrusts abstract reason, centralization and utopian projects.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Burke defends an established aristocracy and hereditary succession of the crown as part of the inherited constitution and says levellers only pervert the natural order.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: Burke holds that a people receives, holds and transmits its government and privileges as it does inherited property, and that no discoveries are to be made in morality.

class-collaboration.rationale: Burke holds that each rank has its place and the state is a partnership of all, and the SEP presents conservatism as organic, against class conflict.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Burke rejects the claim that rulers must be chosen by the people, defending inherited succession and prescription over choosing governors.

decide-locally.rationale: Burke calls love of the little platoon, the local subdivision, the first link of public affection, and the SEP says conservatism puts its faith in family, property and religion rather than the state.

direct-votes.rationale: Burke opposes government by the popular will and holds that those suited by temper and training must rule.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Burke says God willed the state and its connection with the source of perfection, so civil society rests on a divine will, not on a mere contract.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Burke defends hereditary succession of the crown as the settled English constitution, against a right to choose governors.

economic-freedom.rationale: Kirk holds freedom and property closely linked: separate property from private possession and Leviathan becomes master of all (Ten Principles, seventh principle; Conservative Mind, ch. 1, fourth canon).

elective-rulers.rationale: Burke argues at length that a king's title comes from inherited succession and not from the choice of the people, and calls the contrary doctrine absurd.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Kirk holds that the only true forms of equality are equality at the Last Judgment and before a just court of law (Ten Principles, fifth principle), and that the only true equality is moral equality (Conservative Mind, ch. 1, third canon).

equal-outcomes.rationale: Burke says those who attempt to level never equalize, since in every society some description of citizens must be uppermost.

future-generations.rationale: Burke describes the state as a partnership across the dead, the living and those yet to be born, so each generation holds the inheritance in trust.

gradual-change.rationale: Burke holds that a state without the means of some change lacks the means of its conservation, but that change must come by small correction of what exists, never by rebuilding the whole order from first principles.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Burke keeps an established monarchy, aristocracy and democracy together, each in its degree.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Burke resolves to keep an established monarchy alongside the established church, aristocracy and democracy, each in the degree it exists.

morality-needs-religion.rationale: Burke says the English feel that religion is the basis of civil society and the source of all good, and holds that France abandoned virtue along with religion (Reflections).

more-religion-public.rationale: Burke holds that religion is the basis of civil society and the source of all good, and that a state should be consecrated and grounded in religion, as England's established church is (Reflections).

national-church-status.rationale: Burke declares the English resolve to keep an established church and treats the state as joined to religion by divine will.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Burke presents a nation's inherited institutions and manners as a legacy to be received and transmitted to later generations.

property-fundamental.rationale: Burke treats the stability of property as a basic aim of good government and ties liberty to property being secure; the SEP lists private property among the institutions conservatives trust.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Kirk's first canon holds that a narrow rationality cannot of itself satisfy human needs and that political problems are at bottom religious and moral (Conservative Mind, ch. 1); Burke calls man a religious animal and distrusts each man's own stock of reason (Reflections).

religion-illusion.rationale: Burke holds man to be a religious animal and religion a foundation of the civil order, not an illusory comfort.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Burke's Reflections condemns the French Revolution for overturning inherited institutions and wants reform to build on what is inherited.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Weaver defends the Agrarians' view, holding that the link between rural husbandry and political and civic virtue goes back to ancient times and is not mere romantic nostalgia (Southern Essays, The Tennessee Agrarians).

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Burke defends inherited institutions, the nobility and the clergy as the sources of manners and learning, and condemns destroying them to try an experiment.

second-chamber.rationale: Burke defends the House of Peers as formed on the principle of transmitting inherited property and distinction, part of the established constitution alongside the elected Commons (Reflections).

self-interest-moral.rationale: The state is, for Burke, not a partnership for low temporary interest like a trade in pepper and coffee but a bond to be held with reverence.

separate-church-state.rationale: Burke says the state was willed by God together with its connection to the source of all perfection, and defends church establishments against their destruction.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Burke wants change worked in the parts that need it while the established institutions are kept; he rejects decomposing the whole civil mass to originate a new order.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Burke rejects remaking a state's constitution from abstract principles and wants change to proceed from what is inherited.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Burke says man is by constitution a religious animal, that atheism is against reason and instinct, and refuses to let atheism explain or reshape the nation's religious establishment.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Viereck says conservatives and liberals must stand united against totalitarianism, opposing communism and fascism alike (Conservatism From John Adams to Churchill, part 1, Conservatives, Liberals Unite Against Totalitarianism).

universal-morality.rationale: Kirk's first principle is an enduring moral order made for man, with human nature a constant and moral truths permanent (Ten Principles); his first canon is a divine intent ruling society as well as conscience (Conservative Mind, ch. 1).

scope: The American 'New Conservatism' of the 1950s, later called traditionalism, traditionalist conservatism or Burkean conservatism (Henrie, s3): Russell Kirk's The Conservative Mind, with Peter Viereck, Richard Weaver and Robert Nisbet, and the Burkean line of thought they claim as theirs (Burke's Reflections, s4; the Stanford Encyclopedia on tradition and organic society, s2). It holds that political problems are at bottom religious and moral, that a transcendent order or natural law binds government, that custom, prescription and inherited institutions outweigh abstract reasoning, and that change should be gradual and prudent. It excludes the prewar libertarian-leaning conservatism of Mencken, Nock and Babbitt, the fusionist and movement conservatism of Buckley, libertarianism, and neoconservatism, which Henrie and the Law & Liberty essay (s6) distinguish from it.
